title: Rust Login message has multiplexer field not in Go Login
go_ref: /tmp/frp-src/pkg/msg/msg.go — Login struct has no multiplexer field
description: Rust msg::Login has multiplexer: Option<String> which is not present in Go frp's Login struct. This is a Rust extension for TCPMux proxy type detection. Go clients will never set this field, so it will always be None when talking to Go frpc. This does not break interop but is a protocol extension divergence.
fix_suggestion: Document this as a Rust extension field. No code change needed.

title: Rust UdpAddr does not serialize empty Zone field; Go always includes it
description: Rust UdpAddr uses 'skip_serializing_if = String::is_empty' on the Zone field, so empty zones are omitted from JSON. Go's net.UDPAddr always serializes Zone even when empty (producing '"Zone":""'). Both sides can deserialize the other's format (Go tolerates missing Zone; Rust aliases missing Zone to empty string via #[serde(default)]). This is a cosmetic wire difference with no compatibility impact.
fix_suggestion: No change needed. Both formats are interoperable. If wire-identical output is desired, remove the skip_serializing_if on Zone.

title: Go NatHoleResp.DetectBehavior always serialized as non-null struct; Rust uses Option
description: Go's NatHoleResp.DetectBehavior is a value type (NatHoleDetectBehavior) with json:"omitempty" which does NOT omit struct values in Go's encoding/json. Go always sends '"detect_behavior":{}' even when the struct is zero-valued. Rust uses 'Option<NatHoleDetectBehavior>' with skip_serializing_if = Option::is_none, so it omits the field entirely when None. Both sides can deserialize both formats. This is purely cosmetic.
fix_suggestion: No change needed. Both formats are interoperable. If Rust wants to always send the field for wire-identical output, it could use a value type instead of Option.

title: Rust token auth enforces timestamp freshness by default (15s window); Go frp dev does not
go_ref: /tmp/frp-src/pkg/auth/token.go — VerifyLogin only checks MD5(token+timestamp) equality with ConstantTimeEqString; NO timestamp freshness check exists anywhere in Go frp dev
description: Rust login.rs validates timestamp freshness via token_auth_timeout + authentication_timeout (default: 15s) after token hash verification (lines 139-196). Go frp dev at d486018 has NO authentication_timeout field in any config struct — I searched the entire codebase with no matches. Go only does MD5(token+timestamp) comparison. Any Go frpc with clock skew >15s relative to the Rust frps will have its login rejected. This is a Rust-only extension that breaks interop with Go frpc by default.
fix_suggestion: Set ServerConfig.auth.authentication_timeout = 0 and/or auth.token_auth_timeout = false to match Go behavior (no timestamp freshness check). Alternatively, document that Rust frps enforces a 15s clock skew tolerance by default and recommend NTP synchronization.

title: Control replacement lifecycle lacks generation-aware serialization
description: Go frp dev has a complete ControlManager with generation-aware Add/Activate/completeLogin lifecycle. Each runID has a `runMu` serialization lock, monotonically increasing `controlID`, a `handoffBarrier` channel from the old control's doneCh, and registry registration with `RegisterWithControlID`. Rust replaces the old handler by sending `InternalMsg::Shutdown` with no lock-based serialization or barrier. Between the old handler receiving Shutdown and actually cleaning up, both old and new handlers coexist in the same runID map and may concurrently process messages. This can cause lost work connections, duplicate proxy registrations, and stale handler access.
fix_suggestion: Implement a generation-aware ControlManager in Rust that: (a) assigns monotonically increasing control IDs, (b) uses a per-runID lock or oneshot channel to serialize lifecycle transitions, (c) waits for the old handler's done signal before activating the new one, and (d) validates control ID on registry/client operations to prevent stale generations from modifying state.

title: ClientRegistry with control generation awareness missing in Rust
description: Go frp dev's ClientRegistry stores `ControlID` per entry and provides `RegisterWithControlID(key, ..., controlID)` and `MarkOfflineByRunIDAndControlID(runID, controlID)` to prevent stale control generations from modifying registry state after replacement. Rust has no equivalent ClientRegistry — it only has a `run_id_to_ctl_tx` map and a `used_ports` set, with no client-identity-tracking registry. This means: (a) no client metadata (hostname, version, IP, wire protocol) is persisted, (b) the admin API cannot list clients with their metadata, (c) there is no enforcement of unique client_id across connections (Go frp dev returns 'already online' error).
fix_suggestion: Implement a ClientRegistry in Rust matching Go frp dev's registry.go: maintain per-client info (user, clientID, runID, controlID, hostname, version, IP, wireProtocol, online status, timestamps), enforce unique clientID constraint when raw_clientID is non-empty, and accept controlID on register/mark-offline to prevent stale generation writes.

title: Two-phase login (Add-Activate-completeLogin) not implemented in Rust
description: Go frp dev's login flow is: RegisterControl calls Add (admit + set handoff barrier) -> WaitForHandoff (blocks until old control finishes) -> Activate (register with client registry using controlID) -> completeLogin (write LoginResp within locked callback, then start worker). Rust's authenticate() sends LoginResp immediately upon auth success without any two-phase activation or handoff waiting. This means: (a) a new control can send LoginResp before the old control has finished cleanup, (b) two controls can simultaneously be 'active' for the same runID, (c) work connections arriving during the handoff window can be lost or misrouted.
fix_suggestion: Restructure Rust login flow: (1) authenticate and admit the new control (pending state), (2) wait for any old handler's done channel, (3) activate by registering in shared state atomically, then (4) send LoginResp and start the worker loop. Use a oneshot/barrier channel between old and new handlers for handoff synchronization.

title: PublicNetwork feature never detected: server calls classify_nat_feature with empty local_ips
go_ref: pkg/nathole/controller.go:304-312 — ClassifyNATFeature(cm.MappedAddrs, parseIPs(cm.AssistedAddrs)) uses assisted addrs as local_ips
description: The Rust server's control-channel NatHoleVisitor handler calls `classify::classify_nat_feature(&visitor_mapped, &[], &[])` and `classify_nat_feature(&client_mapped, &[], &[])` with empty local_ips slice. The Go controller passes the assisted addresses (parsed as local IPs) as the second argument: ClassifyNATFeature(cm.MappedAddrs, parseIPs(cm.AssistedAddrs)). Without local_ips, `public_network` is always `false`, which breaks mode0 PublicNetwork-aware scoring (Go analysis.go switches sender/receiver scores when a peer is on a public network). The same issue exists in the accept-loop path in handlers.rs (line 643 area).
fix_suggestion: Parse assisted_addrs as local IPs and pass them to classify_nat_feature as the second argument, matching Go's pattern: classify_nat_feature(&mapped_addrs, &parsed_assisted_ips). The Go code calls parseIPs() on AssistedAddrs to extract IPs, then passes them as localIPs param.

title: Rust STUN does not implement CHANGED_ADDRESS / OTHER_ADDR attribute parsing
go_ref: pkg/nathole/discovery.go:114-143 — Go sends second STUN request to resp.otherAddr (changed address), getting a second mapped address from a different server IP
description: Go frp discovery.go sends STUN Binding Requests to both the primary STUN server AND the 'other address' (CHANGED_ADDRESS attribute) to get a second mapped address for improved NAT classification. The Rust STUN implementation only parses MAPPED_ADDRESS (0x0001) and XOR_MAPPED_ADDRESS (0x0020) attributes. It does not parse OTHER-ADDRESS / CHANGED-ADDRESS (0x802c). Rust visitor.rs compensates by sending a second STUN request to the SAME server, but this only proves the NAT mapping is consistent to the same destination IP, not that it changes with different destination IPs. This means NAT classification on the Rust side sees only one external IP, potentially missing port-change-only NAT detection.
fix_suggestion: 1) Add parsing for STUN attribute type 0x802c (OTHER-ADDRESS) in stun.rs parse_binding_response. 2) In visitor.rs, use the other-address from the first STUN response for the second STUN request (matching Go discovery.go:137-138). The Rust visitor.rs currently sends both STUN requests to the same server address.

title: Rust visitor sends mapped_addrs as assisted_addrs instead of local-IP-based assisted addresses
go_ref: pkg/nathole/nathole.go:143-152 — Go Prepare() builds assistedAddrs from local IPs + STUN port, separate from mapped addrs
description: The Rust visitor sends `assisted_addrs: if daa || mapped_addrs.is_empty() { None } else { Some(mapped_addrs) }` — when disable_assisted_addrs is false, it sends the SAME STUN mapped addresses as assisted addresses. Go frp's Prepare() builds assisted addresses from local IPs (ListLocalIPsForNatHole(10)) combined with the STUN port, creating addresses like `local_ip:stun_port` for LAN-based hole punching. The Rust approach sends duplicate data that provides no additional routing information. Go frp's server classifies NAT using `parseIPs(AssistedAddrs)` as local IPs for public_network detection — sending mapped external IPs there would never match local IPs.
fix_suggestion: Implement local IP discovery in the Rust visitor (equivalent of Go's ListLocalIPsForNatHole(10)), filtering IPv4 non-loopback addresses, and combine them with the STUN socket port to form proper assisted addresses. Only then map them to assisted_addrs in NatHoleVisitor.

title: Rust authentication_timeout default (15) differs from comment claim (300) and Go has no such field
go_ref: /tmp/frp-src/pkg/config/v1/server.go — AuthServerConfig has NO authentication_timeout field. Go frp dev has no AuthenticationTimeout anywhere in any config struct.
description: Rust AuthServerConfig defaults authentication_timeout to 15 (line 428 via default_authentication_timeout()). AuthConfig::Default() uses 300 (auth.rs line 152). The auth.rs comment (line 97) claims 'Go frp v0.70.0 default: 900'. But Go frp dev at d486018 has NO authentication_timeout field at all — neither in AuthServerConfig nor AuthClientConfig nor any other config struct. The 900 reference appears to be from old Go legacy config which was removed. This creates confusion about the correct default. The effective default on the server path is 15 (from config), not 300 (from AuthConfig::Default).
fix_suggestion: Remove authentication_timeout entirely from the config structs (matching Go dev which has no such field), or if kept for Rust-only extension, document clearly that Go frp dev does not have this field and set the default comment accurately.

title: Rust server has allow_port_start (10000) / allow_port_end (50000) and max_ports_per_client (50) defaults not in Go
go_ref: /tmp/frp-src/pkg/config/v1/server.go — ServerConfig has AllowPorts []PortsRange but no allow_port_start/allow_port_end or max_ports_per_client defaults
description: Rust ServerConfig has allow_port_start (default 10000), allow_port_end (default 50000), and max_ports_per_client (default 50). Go frp dev has AllowPorts []PortsRange (a list of port range structs, not start/end integers) and MaxPortsPerClient int64 (default 0 = unlimited). These are Rust-specific extensions. The allow_port_start/end at defaults 10000-50000 mean Rust frps rejects proxy ports outside 10000-50000 by default, which would silently break user setups that worked with Go frps (no such restriction).
fix_suggestion: Set allow_port_start/end defaults to match Go (0 or unset = no restriction), or document these as Rust extensions. Consider setting max_ports_per_client to 0 (unlimited) by default to match Go behavior.

title: Rust LoginResp has server_additional_auth_scopes field not present in Go LoginResp
go_ref: /tmp/frp-src/pkg/msg/msg.go — LoginResp struct has only Version, RunID, Error
description: Rust LoginResp has an extra field server_additional_auth_scopes (Option<Vec<String>>) that Go frp's LoginResp does not have. When serialized as JSON, this field will appear in the LoginResp payload sent to the client. While Go JSON decoders ignore unknown fields, this is a protocol deviation. Go LoginResp fields are plain strings (not Option), so they serialize as '' when empty, while Rust uses Option which omits the field entirely when None.
fix_suggestion: Either remove the field to match Go, or tag it with skip_serializing_if = 'Option::is_none' (already done) and document it as a Rust extension. Ensure Go clients can safely ignore this extra field.

title: Rust tcp_mux feature flag inconsistency between client and server defaults
go_ref: /tmp/frp-src/pkg/config/v1/server.go ServerTransportConfig.Complete() and client.go ClientTransportConfig.Complete() — both unconditionally default TCPMux to true
description: Both Rust ClientConfig and ServerConfig/ServerTransportConfig use default_tcp_mux() = cfg!(feature = 'tcp-mux'). This means the tcp_mux default depends on compile-time feature selection, not the configuration. If server and client are compiled with different feature flags, they would have different defaults for tcp_mux — Go behavior is always true on both sides.
fix_suggestion: Change to unconditional true default, or ensure the tcp-mux feature is always enabled in Cargo.toml and document this dependency.

title: Rust V2 handshake preferred_aead_algorithms does not match Go conditional hardware detection
go_ref: /tmp/frp-src/pkg/proto/wire/crypto.go PreferredAEADAlgorithms() — orders AES-256-GCM first only on x86_64/arm64/s390x with AES-NI; XChaCha20-Poly1305 first otherwise
description: Go frp dev's PreferredAEADAlgorithms() checks CPU capabilities (AES-NI, PCLMULQDQ, etc.) to determine whether to prefer AES-256-GCM or XChaCha20-Poly1305 first. Rust's preferred_aead_algorithms() unconditionally returns [AES-256-GCM, XChaCha20-Poly1305] (or just [AES-256-GCM] if chacha20 feature is disabled). This means Rust always advertises AES-256-GCM as preferred, even on hardware without AES acceleration, where Go would prefer XChaCha20-Poly1305 on the same hardware. The final algorithm selection is done by the server, so this only affects the client's offer order — the server picks, so in practice the server on similar hardware will select the same algorithm. But a Rust frps running on ARM without crypto extensions would still select AES-256-GCM, while Go would prefer XChaCha20-Poly1305.
fix_suggestion: Update preferred_aead_algorithms() to check for AES-NI/PCLMULQDQ (x86), AES/PMULL (ARM64) and prefer XChaCha20-Poly1305 when hardware acceleration is unavailable, matching Go's behavior.

title: Rust V2 HKDF AEAD key derivation uses token as IKM (raw bytes); Go does the same
description: Both Go and Rust use the token bytes directly as IKM (input key material) for HKDF-SHA256, with transcript_hash as salt. This is correct and matches. However, Rust uses the token string's raw UTF-8 bytes (token.as_bytes()) while Go passes the []byte slice from the auth key. Both are effectively the same since the token is ASCII/UTF-8 in both implementations.
fix_suggestion: No change needed — implementations are functionally identical.

title: Yamux keepalive uses polling fallback instead of native yamux keepalive interval
description: Go frp sets `fmuxCfg.KeepAliveInterval` on the yamux config (hashicorp/yamux fork) to the configured value (default 30s). Rust mux.rs line 119-121 notes: 'NOTE: yamux 0.14.0 does not expose set_keepalive_interval on Config.' Rust implements keepalive via a `tokio::time::sleep(keepalive)` branch in the select! loop that drives the yamux connection (this triggers poll_next_inbound periodically). The behavior is functionally similar (both detect dead peers) but uses a different mechanism. Under sustained load, Rust's approach adds an extra timer wakeup per keepalive interval. Under idle, both approaches are equivalent.
fix_suggestion: Monitor yamux-rs for API additions that expose keepalive_interval natively. Until then, the polling fallback is acceptable but should be documented more clearly as a behavioral divergence.

title: QUIC_GO_DISABLE_ECN and crypto.DefaultSalt env vars not configured in Rust
description: Go frp's init() function sets `crypto.DefaultSalt = "frp"` (used by golib/crypto for AES-128-CFB control encryption key derivation) and disables QUIC ECN by default due to known issues on certain OSes. Rust uses `frp-core::encryption::derive_key()` for the AES key and `quinn` for QUIC (not quic-go). The quinn library may handle ECN differently, but there is no explicit equivalent to Go frp's ECN disabling. Additionally, Go frp disables quic-go's receive buffer warning.
fix_suggestion: Ensure the encryption key derivation (`derive_key`) produces identical results to Go frp's `golib/crypto` with DefaultSalt="frp". The QUIC ECN handling in quinn should be checked — if quinn enables ECN by default, consider disabling it for parity.

title: Go frp's ClientCommonConfig.Complete() defaults missing in Rust config
go_ref: /tmp/frp-src/pkg/config/v1/client.go (Complete() method sets TCPMux defaults, poolCount, etc.) and server.go Complete() lines 182-197
description: Go frp has a `Complete()` method on config structs that fills in defaults (e.g., TCPMux default true, TCPMuxKeepaliveInterval default 30, TCPKeepAlive default 7200, HeartbeatTimeout default 90 or -1 depending on TCPMux). Rust's config.rs uses serde defaults. Some values match serde defaults (tcp_mux defaults to true in Rust), but the conditional logic (HeartbeatTimeout = -1 when TCPMux enabled) is not replicated. Config defaults may diverge subtly between the two implementations.
fix_suggestion: Audit all numeric/boolean config defaults in frp-core/src/config.rs against Go frp v1 Complete() methods. Ensure the conditional logic (especially for HeartbeatTimeout and TCPMux interaction) is replicated in Rust's default path.

title: Rust HTTP health check sends HTTP/1.0 requests; Go frp sends proper HTTP/1.1
go_ref: /tmp/frp-src/client/health/health.go lines 167-184: http.NewRequestWithContext with http.DefaultClient.Do (proper HTTP client, HTTP/1.1 defaults)
description: Go frp's HTTP health check uses `http.NewRequestWithContext()` and `http.DefaultClient.Do()`, which sends proper HTTP/1.1 requests with full header support. Rust's `run_http_check` constructs a raw HTTP/1.0 GET request manually and only checks for '200' or ' 2' in the status line. The raw approach handles most cases but may not handle chunked responses, keep-alive connections, or redirects. The Host header is also derived from addr.split(':')[0] which may strip port info.
fix_suggestion: Consider using an HTTP client crate (like `reqwest`) for HTTP health checks, or enhance the raw parser to handle HTTP/1.1 responses properly (chunked encoding, connection: close, etc.). At minimum, add port to the Host header.

title: Rust WebSocket handler relies on raw manual framing for Go frp compat — diverges from Go frp's use of golang.org/x/net/websocket
go_ref: /tmp/frp-src/pkg/util/net/websocket.go (WebsocketListener, BinaryFrame payload type), dial.go (DialHookWebsocket with cfg.PayloadType = websocket.BinaryFrame)
description: Go frp uses `golang.org/x/net/websocket` library which sends encrypted frp data as TEXT frames (violating RFC 6455 §5.6 for non-UTF-8 payloads). Rust implements a custom WsByteStream with two modes: tungstenite (client side, sends Binary frames) and Raw (server/manual mode, handles both text and binary frames). The Raw mode is specifically designed to handle Go frp's non-UTF-8 text frames. Rust's client mode (tungstenite) sends Binary frames, which Go frp's server WsByteStream will accept. The interop should work but the Rust approach is much more complex and fragile.
fix_suggestion: The existing Raw frame handling is correct for interop. However, the code (entire WsByteStream implementation plus accept_websocket/accept_websocket_from_peeked/connect_ws_raw) is nearly 800 lines of manual WebSocket frame parsing. Consider testing against Go frps with various payload patterns (binary, encrypted, compressed) to ensure edge cases are handled.

title: Login throttle is Rust-only, not present in Go frp dev
description: Rust implements per-IP login throttling (5 failed attempts per 60s) with synthetic IP hashing for non-TCP transports. Go frp dev has no equivalent. This is an extra security feature in Rust but means Rust may reject legitimate rapid reconnections that Go frp would accept (e.g., during frpc crash loops). The throttle also reserves an attempt slot before authentication completes, so a single authentication failure consumes one of the 5 slots.
fix_suggestion: Document the throttle behavior. Consider whether the throttle should only count authentication failures (not reservations) to match expected security posture. Make the throttle configurable or disabled by default for Go frp compat.

title: Timestamp-based replay protection is Rust-only
go_ref: server/control.go (no timestamp dedup; relies on auth.VerifyLogin)
description: Rust implements replay attack protection by tracking (timestamp, run_id) pairs in a BTreeMap with split_off cleanup. Go frp dev does not have this mechanism, relying solely on auth token validation and timestamp freshness in the auth verifier. This adds an extra layer of defense in Rust but introduces a dependency on client-provided run_id for effective dedup. When run_id is empty, Rust generates a UUID that is never reused, making the dedup ineffective. This finding flags a behavioral difference for interoperability testing.
fix_suggestion: Document that the replay protection is best-effort when clients don't supply a stable run_id. Consider whether Go frpc sends run_id in Login messages consistently (it does for reconnections with the same run_id).

title: ServerMetrics NewProxy signature includes user/clientID in Go frp dev
description: Go frp dev's metrics server.NewProxy() receives `user` and `clientID` parameters. Rust's proxy_metrics tracking does not include user or clientID dimensions. This means admin API responses that require per-user or per-client proxy categorization may return incomplete data. The Go frp dev mem stats collector tracks proxy_type_counts and client_counts which depend on these parameters.
fix_suggestion: Add user and clientID fields to the proxy metrics registry in Rust. Update NewProxy calls in proxy_ops.rs to pass the user (from ControlTx.user) and clientID (from run_id) when creating metrics entries.

title: healthz readiness probe differs from Go frp dev's simple healthz
description: Go frp dev's /healthz always returns HTTP 200 with no body. Rust's /healthz supports both 'liveness' (default, returns 200 OK) and 'readiness' (checks shutdown token, lock contention on used_ports, run_id_to_ctl_tx, and proxy_manager). The readiness check is a Rust-only enhancement but could cause load balancers to report the server as unhealthy when it would be considered healthy by Go frp standards, particularly under lock contention.
fix_suggestion: Ensure the default /healthz (no probe param) always returns 200 for Go frp compat. Document that the readiness probe is a Rust-specific enhancement and may need adjusted thresholds in production.

title: Rust v2 dashboard API sends ServerAdditionalAuthScopes in error LoginResp
go_ref: server/service.go:497-499 (no extra field in error LoginResp)
description: Go frp dev's LoginResp error responses include only Version, RunID (empty), and Error. Rust's error LoginResp includes server_additional_auth_scopes even on error responses. This is harmless (Go clients ignore unknown fields) but differs from expected Go frp dev wire format. The extra field could confuse packet-capture analysis or protocol conformance tests.
fix_suggestion: Only include server_additional_auth_scopes in successful LoginResp, matching Go frp dev behavior. Set it to None in error responses.

title: Rust Login message has extra field 'multiplexer' not present in Go Login
description: Rust Login struct contains a 'multiplexer: Option<String>' field that does not exist in Go's Login struct. Go's JSON decoder silently ignores unknown fields, so this does not cause deserialization errors. However, the field pollutes the wire with data Go does not use. 'multiplexer' IS a valid field in Go's NewProxy message (msg.go:133), so its presence in Login may indicate a copy-paste error or design intent mismatch.
fix_suggestion: Verify that 'multiplexer' in Login is intentional. If not, remove it from the Rust Login struct. If it is intended as a forward-compatibility field, add a comment explaining why.

title: Rust LoginResp has extra field 'serverAdditionalAuthScopes' not present in Go LoginResp
description: Rust LoginResp defines 'server_additional_auth_scopes: Option<Vec<String>>' with serde rename 'serverAdditionalAuthScopes'. This field does not exist in Go frp dev's LoginResp struct. Go silently ignores unknown JSON fields. The field appears to anticipate a future Go feature (scoped authentication for heartbeat and work connection messages) that does not yet exist in the Go codebase.
fix_suggestion: Either gate this field behind a feature flag, or document that it is a forward-compatibility placeholder for a not-yet-implemented Go feature. Ensure Rust never sets a non-None value when talking to a Go peer.

title: Rust NewProxy has extra fields not present in Go NewProxy
description: Rust NewProxy struct contains 7 fields not present in Go frp dev's NewProxy: 'local_str', 'virtual_net', 'proxy_protocol_version', 'advertise_subnet', 'vnet_ip', 'vnet_netmask', 'vnet_mtu'. 'proxy_protocol_version' exists as a transport config concept in Go but is not a wire field in the NewProxy message. 'virtual_net' is a Go plugin type but not a NewProxy wire field. The remaining VNet fields ('vnet_ip', 'vnet_netmask', 'vnet_mtu', 'advertise_subnet') have no Go equivalents at all. Go silently ignores unknown fields.
fix_suggestion: Gate VNet-specific fields behind the 'vnet' feature flag like the VnetRouteAdvertise/VnetPacket/VnetRouteRemove message types. Remove 'local_str' if it is dead code. Consider whether 'proxy_protocol_version' should be removed or promoted to an actual Go-compatible field.

title: Rust StartWorkConn has extra fields not present in Go StartWorkConn
description: Rust StartWorkConn has 5 fields not in Go's StartWorkConn: 'use_encryption: Option<bool>', 'use_compression: Option<bool>', 'nat_hole_sid: Option<String>', 'nat_hole_visitor_addr: Option<String>', 'sk: Option<String>'. Go's StartWorkConn only has: proxy_name, src_addr, dst_addr, src_port, dst_port, error. Go silently ignores extra JSON fields. These fields exist in Go's NewProxy and NewVisitorConn but not in StartWorkConn.
fix_suggestion: Verify these extra fields are needed for Rust-internal communication purposes. If they are intended to be sent to Go peers, they will be silently ignored. Consider whether 'use_encryption' and 'use_compression' should be removed since Go conveys this information via the proxier metadata, not via StartWorkConn.

title: Rust NatHoleClient has extra fields not present in Go NatHoleClient
description: Rust NatHoleClient has 2 fields not in Go frp dev's NatHoleClient: 'protocol: Option<String>' and 'visitor_addr: Option<String>'. Go's NatHoleClient only has: transaction_id, proxy_name, sid, mapped_addrs, assisted_addrs. Go silently ignores unknown JSON fields.
fix_suggestion: Verify these fields are needed for Rust-internal NAT hole punching. If they are meant to be forwarded to Go peers, they will be silently ignored. Document why they exist.

title: Go NatHoleDetectBehavior JSON key 'read_timeout' (not 'read_timeout_ms') is handled correctly by Rust alias
description: Go's NatHoleDetectBehavior uses JSON key 'read_timeout' (not 'read_timeout_ms') for the read timeout field. Rust handles this correctly with 'rename = "read_timeout", alias = "read_timeout_ms". This is correct, not a bug. Flagged because the field name and JSON tag differ from the Rust struct field name. Verified compatible.
fix_suggestion: No change needed. The serde attributes correctly match Go's wire format.

title: Go StartWorkConn uses uint16 for ports; Rust uses i32 — compatible but type-mismatched
description: Go StartWorkConn declares SrcPort and DstPort as uint16 (0-65535). Rust declares src_port and dst_port as Option<i32>. JSON serialization uses the same numeric representation for values 0-65535. However, if Rust ever sets a port value outside the uint16 range (>65535 or negative), it would be a protocol mismatch. Currently this cannot happen because ports are always in the valid range.
fix_suggestion: Consider changing Rust port fields to Option<u16> to match Go's type semantics and prevent accidental out-of-range values.

title: PreCheck timeout degrades gracefully (proceeds with full request) instead of failing — Go returns error immediately
go_ref: pkg/nathole/nathole.go:88-115 — PreCheck returns error on timeout or invalid response, does not fall through
description: Rust visitor's PreCheck phase (lines 128-181) sends a pre_check NatHoleVisitor and waits up to 15s for a response. If it times out, the code falls through with a warning and proceeds with the full STUN + NatHoleVisitor exchange. Go's PreCheck returns an error immediately. The Rust approach is more resilient but means Rust frpc will do STUN and hole-punch attempts even against servers that don't support PreCheck, which wastes resources. This is a design difference, not a bug, but it means Rust behavior diverges from Go.
fix_suggestion: Document this as an intentional design choice (graceful degradation for older servers).

title: Rust STUN timeout (5s) differs from Go responseTimeout (3s)
description: Go uses a 3-second responseTimeout for STUN requests. Rust uses 5 seconds across all stun_binding* functions. Both should be sufficient for local network STUN servers. The longer timeout in Rust is more tolerant of slow networks but increases the worst-case STUN delay.
fix_suggestion: Reduce Rust STUN timeout to 3s for wire-compatible timing, or make it configurable.

title: Rust NatHoleDetectSid sends empty nonce string vs Go random digit string
go_ref: pkg/nathole/nathole.go:353 — Nonce: strings.Repeat("0", rand.IntN(20)) (Go uses 0-19 zeros as nonce in side-channel detection)
description: The Rust `NatHoleDetectSid::new()` sets `nonce: String::new()` (always empty). Go's `sendSidMessage` sets `Nonce: strings.Repeat("0", rand.IntN(20))` which is a random-length string of zeros (0-19 chars). The nonce is only used for side-channel detection (response matching) and has no security significance. Both sides treat an empty nonce as valid. Wire compatible but not timing-compatible.
fix_suggestion: Add random nonce generation matching Go's behavior for reproducibility.

title: NAT_HOLE_TIMEOUT constant same value (10) as Go but used differently
description: Both Go and Rust define NAT_HOLE_TIMEOUT = 10 (seconds). Go uses this as `time.Duration(NatHoleTimeout) * time.Second` in select timeout. Rust uses it as `Duration::from_secs(NAT_HOLE_TIMEOUT)` in the spawn task timeout for waiting on the provider's NatHoleClient. Implementations match.
fix_suggestion: No fix needed — this is correctly implemented.

title: Rust sk_index race condition fix documented (CLAUDE.md line 242) — Go does not have this issue
go_ref: server/proxy/proxy.go:200 — startVisitorListener pre-registers listener during Run(), before registration returns
description: CLAUDE.md documents that STCP/XTCP visitors may send NewVisitorConn before the server's proxy_manager.register() completes. Go frp avoids this by pre-registering the visitor listener during proxy.Run() (startVisitorListener → rc.VisitorManager.Listen()) before the proxy registration returns to the control. Rust uses sk_index as a fallback in both handlers.rs and control/nathole.rs when proxy_manager.get() returns None. This is not a bug — it's a documented design divergence with Rust's sk_index fallback.
fix_suggestion: No fix needed — the race condition fix is already implemented via sk_index fallback.

title: Go discovery_test.go has 382 lines of STUN tests — Rust stun.rs has no end-to-end STUN integration test
go_ref: pkg/nathole/discovery_test.go — Tests STUN exchange with real UDP sockets, NAT classification after discovery, malformed/error responses, timeout behavior, and client socket lifecycle
description: Go frp dev added 382 lines of integration tests for the STUN discovery flow in discovery_test.go, covering: Discover reuses local port, NAT classification after STUN, legacy MAPPED-ADDRESS vs XOR-MAPPED-ADDRESS precedence, STUN errors, timeouts, and socket deadline interaction. Rust stun.rs has unit tests for attribute parsing, XOR-MAPPED-ADDRESS, and binding response parsing, but NO end-to-end test that exercises the full discover→classify pipeline with a real UDP socket. The discovery_test.go file was added in the Go dev branch and is the most important new testing surface.
fix_suggestion: Add a Rust integration test for the full STUN discovery + NAT classification pipeline, matching Go's TestDiscoverReusesLocalPortAndPreservesNATClassification and TestDoSTUNRequestMapsLegacyAndModernAddresses. Use a local UDP STUN server similar to Go's serveOneSTUNRequest/listenTestUDP4 pattern.

title: Rust heartbeat_interval defaults unconditionally to 30; Go conditionally sets to -1 when tcp_mux is enabled
go_ref: /tmp/frp-src/pkg/config/v1/client.go ClientTransportConfig.Complete() line 156-159: when TCPMux=true, HeartbeatInterval defaults to -1 (disabled)
description: Go ClientTransportConfig.Complete() conditionally sets HeartbeatInterval=-1 when TCPMux is enabled (relying on tcpmux keepalive instead), and HeartbeatInterval=30 only when TCPMux is disabled. Rust ClientConfig defaults heartbeat_interval unconditionally to 30 regardless of tcp_mux setting. This means Rust clients send application-layer heartbeats every 30s even when tcp_mux is active, while Go clients do not. The Rust server control loop also sends Pings every 10s unconditionally (login.rs line 442). This is a behavioral divergence — both sides work, but Rust generates unnecessary extra heartbeat traffic when tcp_mux is enabled.
fix_suggestion: Apply the same conditional default logic as Go: if tcp_mux is true, set heartbeat_interval to -1 (disabled) as the default. This can be done in a ClientConfig::complete() method called after deserialization.

title: Rust nat_hole_stun_server defaults to empty string; Go defaults to 'stun.easyvoip.com:3478'
description: Go frp dev defaults NatHoleSTUNServer to 'stun.easyvoip.com:3478'. Rust ClientConfig defaults nat_hole_stun_server to empty string (serde default for String). When empty, STUN-based NAT hole punching will not work unless the user explicitly configures a STUN server. This breaks NAT traversal for XTCP proxies requiring STUN-based address discovery.
fix_suggestion: Change the default of nat_hole_stun_server to 'stun.easyvoip.com:3478' to match Go frp behavior, or apply the default in a post-deserialization Complete() step.

title: Rust tcp_mux default depends on compile-time feature flag; Go unconditionally defaults to true
description: Rust default_tcp_mux() returns cfg!(feature = 'tcp-mux') — true only when the tcp-mux crate feature is compiled in. Go unconditionally defaults TCPMux to true. If the Rust binary is compiled without the tcp-mux feature (unusual but possible), multiplexing is off by default, which would cause connection failures with Go clients expecting tcp_mux by default.
fix_suggestion: Change default_tcp_mux() to unconditionally return true, matching Go behavior. The feature flag can still gate the implementation at compile time, but the default should be true regardless.

title: Rust proxy_bind_addr defaults to empty string; Go inherits from bind_addr
go_ref: /tmp/frp-src/pkg/config/v1/server.go ServerConfig.Complete() lines 112-113: if ProxyBindAddr == '', set to BindAddr
description: Go ServerConfig.Complete() sets ProxyBindAddr = BindAddr when ProxyBindAddr is empty. Rust's proxy_bind_addr defaults to '' with no fallback logic. If the application code doesn't handle this fallback, proxy listeners may bind to an incorrect address (potentially 0.0.0.0 instead of inheriting from bind_addr, or what Go would do).
fix_suggestion: Add a ServerConfig::complete() method or application-level initialization that defaults proxy_bind_addr to bind_addr when empty, matching Go behavior.

title: Missing heartbeat timeout detection — Rust sends pings but does not track pong timeout
description: Go frp tracks `lastPong` time and checks it against `HeartbeatTimeout` (default 90s; set to -1 when TCPMux is enabled). If `time.Since(lastPong) > HeartbeatTimeout`, Go warns 'heartbeat timeout' and eventually reconnects. Rust's service.rs only sends pings at `heartbeat_interval` via a `tokio::time::interval` timer (line 968) and logs 'Ping sent' / 'Pong received' but never checks the elapsed time since the last Pong. A dead control connection with a responsive TCP stack (no RST) would go undetected until the next write fails.
fix_suggestion: Add a `last_pong: Instant` field, update it on receiving Pong, and spawn a watchdog task/select branch that triggers reconnect if `last_pong.elapsed() > heartbeat_timeout`. Respect Go's convention of disabling heartbeat timeout when TCPMux is enabled (yamux provides its own keepalive).

title: Missing proxy phase state machine for lifecycle tracking
go_ref: /tmp/frp-src/client/proxy/proxy_wrapper.go lines 38-51 (ProxyPhase* constants), lines 138-164 (SetRunningStatus, Start, Stop), lines 194-239 (checkWorker)
description: Go frp maintains a detailed proxy phase state machine: New → WaitStart → StartErr/Running → CheckFailed → Closed. This controls when proxies are registered with the server, handles retries on start error, and integrates with health checks. Rust's ProxyRuntimeInfo stores only a generic `err: String` and `remote_addr: String` without any phase tracking. Proxies are registered once during login, and failures are stored as error strings with no retry cycle. This means a proxy that fails registration is never retried during the session.
fix_suggestion: Add a ProxyPhase enum to ProxyRuntimeInfo (New, WaitStart, Running, CheckFailed, Closed) and a check_worker-style background task that retries failed proxy registrations. Match Go frp's behavior where `checkWorker` periodically transitions New/CheckFailed proxies back to WaitStart to retry registration.

title: KCP XOR encryption comment in session.rs is misleading — Go frp does not use KCP-level encryption
go_ref: /tmp/frp-src/pkg/util/net/kcp.go lines 31, 96 (kcp.ListenWithOptions with nil blockCrypt, NewConn3 with nil blockCrypt)
description: Rust session.rs line 10-11 reads: 'XOR encryption (`kcp_compat::XorBlock`) is NOT yet wired — KcpConfig lacks a crypt field'. This implies a gap in KCP interop, but Go frp's kcp.go passes `nil` for the blockCrypt parameter in both `kcp.ListenWithOptions()` and `kcp.NewConn3()`, meaning NO KCP-level encryption is used. The `kcp-go` library supports BlockCrypt (XOR, AES, Blowfish, etc.) but frp itself never enables it. The comment incorrectly flags a non-existent interop gap.
fix_suggestion: Update the comment in session.rs and/or the CHANGELOG to clarify that Go frp does NOT use KCP block encryption. The `kcp_compat::XorBlock` code is unused dead code unless frp-rs decides to add a proprietary KCP encryption extension (which would break interop with Go frp).

title: Group health check TODO describes a feature that does not exist in Go frp
go_ref: /tmp/frp-src/pkg/config/v1/proxy.go lines 72-106 (HealthCheckConfig with Type: "" | "tcp" | "http"), /tmp/frp-src/pkg/config/v1/validation/proxy.go lines 49-54 (validation rejects anything other than "", "tcp", "http")
description: Rust health.rs lines 10-26 contain a TODO: 'group health check (Go frp compat gap) ... When health_check_type == "group"'. However, Go frp's validation logic (validation/proxy.go:49-54) only accepts health check types of "", "tcp", or "http". There is no "group" health check type in Go frp dev. Health checks are per-proxy only; the proxy Group field (proxy.go:53) is used solely for server-side load balancing, not health checking. The TODO describes a feature that would not interoperate with Go frp.
fix_suggestion: Remove the group health check TODO comment or update it to reflect that Go frp does not support group-level health checks. If group-level health checking is desired as a frp-rs extension, document it as such (not as a Go compat gap).

title: Missing config store / CRUD API for runtime proxy/visitor management
go_ref: /tmp/frp-src/client/config_manager.go lines 153-464 (ListStoreProxies, CreateStoreProxy, UpdateStoreProxy, DeleteStoreProxy, etc. — full CRUD on StoreSource proxies and visitors)
description: Go frp dev has a complete `config_manager.go` with `StoreSource` that supports CRUD operations on proxies and visitors (CreateStoreProxy, UpdateStoreProxy, DeleteStoreProxy, ListStoreProxies, etc.), config source aggregation, and hot-reload via the admin API. These are exposed through the admin HTTP API. Rust's reload.rs only implements `do_reload()` which diffs old vs new config from file. There is no store/CRUD mechanism, no config source aggregation, and no persistence layer. The admin API endpoints for proxy CRUD are therefore non-functional.
fix_suggestion: Implement a StoreSource trait with in-memory HashMap storage (matching Go frp's source.StoreSource interface) and wire it through the admin API. The CRUD operations should trigger config reload (via the existing reload channel) after each mutation.

title: TCP group load balancing allocates per-proxy ports instead of shared port
description: Go frp dev's TCPGroupCtl creates a shared listener on one port for all proxies in the same load-balancer group, with round-robin dispatch. Rust's proxy_ops.rs `listen_and_proxy` spawns an independent TCP listener per proxy, even when proxies belong to a group. Each proxy gets its own port via `allocate_port_multi`. The group load balancing in pool.rs `handle_proxy_user_conn` selects a backend but the connection arrives on the selected proxy's own port, not a shared group port. This changes the port allocation behavior for TCP groups and may cause port exhaustion or conflict with expected frpc configuration.
fix_suggestion: Implement a TCP group controller in Rust that creates a shared listener per group on a single port and dispatches incoming connections to group members via the InternalMsg::ProxyUserConn channel. Register proxies into the group controller during handle_new_proxy when group is non-empty, similar to Go frp dev's TCPGroupCtl.

title: HTTP group health check awareness missing in Rust load balancer
description: Go frp dev's HTTPGroupController has health-check-aware endpoint selection: `chooseEndpoint`/`chooseCreateConn` delegates to `createConnByEndpoint` with round-robin over registered proxies, and the vhost router tracks 'healthy' status via back-end health check probes. Rust's group load balancing in `handle_proxy_user_conn` calls `select_group_backend` with no health check filtering — it picks the next backend in round-robin regardless of online/offline status. When a backend proxy is unhealthy, Rust may still route traffic to it, causing connection failures that Go frp would avoid.
fix_suggestion: Add health status tracking to the proxy manager (e.g., a last-failure timestamp or explicit online/offline flag). Update select_group_backend to skip unhealthy backends. Add a periodic health check task that marks proxies as unhealthy after connection failures and recovers them after a cooldown period.

title: Server-side bandwidth limit mode semantics differ from Go frp
description: Go frp dev applies server-side rate limiting only when `BandwidthLimitMode == BandwidthLimitModeServer` (the string 'server'). Rust checks for both 'client' and 'both' modes. When `BandwidthLimitMode` is set to 'both' or 'client' in the frpc config, Rust creates bandwidth limiters while Go frp dev does not (or creates them but with different semantics). This means client-side bandwidth limits configured in Rust may unexpectedly consume server CPU for rate limiting, or the server-side limiting may behave differently when the client sends 'both' mode.
fix_suggestion: Match Go frp dev behavior: only create server-side bandwidth limiters when bandwidth_limit_mode is 'server'. For 'client' mode, trust the client to apply its own limits. For 'both' mode, Go frp dev does not handle it; decide whether to add Go-compatible 'both' semantics or reject unsupported modes.

title: ClientSpec.AlwaysAuthPass for internal connections not supported
description: Go frp dev allows internal connections (SSH tunnel gateway) with `ClientSpec.AlwaysAuthPass` to bypass authentication by substituting an AlwaysPassVerifier. Rust's login.rs authenticate() always validates the token (or returns an error) regardless of any internal connection flag. The SSH tunnel gateway in Rust does not pass an 'internal' flag to the control handler. This could cause SSH tunnel gateway connections to fail authentication if the token is not configured identically on both sides.
fix_suggestion: Add an 'internal' flag to the control handler path that, when set, uses an AlwaysPassVerifier for auth. Thread this flag from the SSH gateway into handle_control (via the Login message or a separate parameter), similar to Go frp dev's AlwaysAuthPass in ClientSpec.

title: ServerAdditionalAuthScopes in LoginResp differs from Go frp
description: Go frp dev's LoginResp struct does NOT have a ServerAdditionalAuthScopes field (checked in pkg/msg/msg.go: type LoginResp struct { Version, RunID, Error }). Rust's LoginResp includes `server_additional_auth_scopes` and authenticates() sends `Some(["HeartBeats", "NewWorkConns"])`. While Go clients ignore unknown JSON fields, this means Rust requires additional auth on HeartBeats and NewWorkConns messages by default, whereas Go frp dev does not. Rust frp clients handle this, but third-party clients or older Go frpc versions may not expect auth on HeartBeats and break.
fix_suggestion: Either: (a) make server_additional_auth_scopes configurable with a Go-compatible default (empty/none), or (b) add a compatibility mode where additional_auth_scopes are empty for Go frpc interop. Document that Rust requires auth on those message types when this scopes list is non-empty.

title: Work connection pool lacks idle timeout configuration in Go frp dev
description: Rust implements a configurable idle timeout for pooled work connections that Go frp dev does not have. Rust's `pool_idle_timeout` (from state.pool.idle_timeout) periodically evicts stale entries from the work pool. This is a strict superset of Go frp behavior, but if the idle timeout is misconfigured or too aggressive, it could cause unnecessary work connection churn that Go frp would not exhibit. The feature itself is beneficial; this finding flags the behavioral difference for interoperability testing.
fix_suggestion: Ensure idle_timeout defaults to 0 (disabled) for Go frp compat. Document the configuration option if exposed to users so they understand it is a Rust-only feature.

title: Proxy NewProxyResp includes response_headers fields not handled in Rust inline bridge
go_ref: server/proxy/http.go:63 (ResponseHeaders config in vhost route config)
description: Go frp dev injects response headers at the vhost reverse proxy level (via vhost RouteConfig.ResponseHeaders). Rust's bridge.rs handles response_headers via ResponseHeaderInjector only when `req.proxy_type.starts_with('http')` and `use_enc` is true (line 462-481) or when bandwidth limiting is active (line 681-694). For the fast path (plain relay without encryption, bandwidth limit, or response_headers), Rust uses `relay_plain_fast` / `copy_bidirectional` which bypasses header injection entirely. This means HTTP response headers configured in NewProxy will not be injected for proxies without encryption or rate limiting.
fix_suggestion: Move response_header injection earlier in the bridge pipeline so it always applies for HTTP proxy types, regardless of encryption/rate-limiting settings. Use the ResponseHeaderInjector wrapper unconditionally for HTTP proxy types.

title: Rust-only V1 type bytes 0x37 ('7') and 0x38 ('8') not recognized by Go
description: Rust defines TYPE_CLOSE_PROXY_RESP (0x37 = '7') and TYPE_ERROR (0x38 = '8') as V1 type byte constants. Go frp dev only registers types through type byte '6'. If Rust ever sends either message to a Go peer over V1, Go will return 'unknown type byte' and close the connection. Currently these are not sent to Go peers (confirmed by code audit), but the type bytes occupy the ASCII '7' and '8' slots which Go could assign in the future, creating a conflict.
fix_suggestion: Keep the internal-only guard (comments at protocol.rs line 12-14 are clear). Consider adding a runtime assertion in write_msg_v1 that panics if the target is a Go-compatible peer and the message is CloseProxyResp or Error. Add a crate-level compile-time check that these type bytes do not collide with any future Go dev additions.

title: Rust-only V2 type IDs 19 and 20 not recognized by Go
description: Rust assigns V2_TYPE_CLOSE_PROXY_RESP = 19 and V2_TYPE_ERROR = 20 as V2 type IDs. Go frp dev only registers V2 type IDs 1-18. If Rust sends either message over V2 to a Go peer, Go will reject with 'unknown v2 message type'. These IDs are just below the V2 VNet range (42-44) so future Go assignments should be safe, but Rust needs to ensure these are never dispatched to Go peers.
fix_suggestion: Same as V1 fix: add runtime guards in write_msg_v2. Document that IDs 19-20 are reserved for Rust extension and should not be used by Go.

title: Rust NatHoleClient.sid is Option<String> vs Go's required string — wire compatible but semantically different
go_ref: pkg/msg/msg.go NatHoleClient struct uses `Sid string json:"sid,omitempty"`
description: Go's NatHoleClient has `Sid string` tagged omitempty — empty string is omitted from JSON. Rust has `sid: Option<String>` with skip_serializing_if. When Rust sends NatHoleClient with sid=None, Go receives empty string (zero value), which is fine for Go's `if m.Sid == ""` checks. However, when Rust receives Go's NatHoleClient that has sid populated, Rust deserializes it as Some(sid). This is wire-compatible, but the Rust code has a struct NatHoleClient with sid where Sid is missing for Go sessions — this could cause Rust server-side bugs.
fix_suggestion: Change Rust NatHoleClient.sid to a plain String (not Option) to match Go's semantics exactly.

title: Rust gen_analysis_key uses canonical string format while Go uses MD5 hash — incompatible between implementations
go_ref: pkg/nathole/controller.go:74-91 — genAnalysisKey() writes to md5.New(), incorporating first IP, NAT type, behavior, and regular_ports_change
description: Go frp genAnalysisKey() computes `md5(visitor_first_ip + v_nat_type + v_behavior + v_regular + client_first_ip + c_nat_type + c_behavior + c_regular)` as a hex-encoded 32-character string. Rust gen_analysis_key() produces `"nat_type:behavior:regular|nat_type:behavior:regular"` as a canonical string. Both are consumed only within their own Analyzer instances (server-local), so this does not break cross-implementation wire protocol. However, if a future deployment mixes Go and Rust frpc against a shared Go+Rust frps cluster, the analysis data would be fragmented.
fix_suggestion: Recommend only as a future compatibility enhancement. For now, both implementations work independently because the analyzer is per-server-process.

title: Rust handle_nat_hole_resp creates a synthetic NatHoleClient from NatHoleResp and calls handle_client — may double-signal the session notify channel
go_ref: pkg/nathole/controller.go — Go server does NOT call HandleClient when receiving NatHoleResp; it only stores the response for later sending via Send()
description: The Rust `handle_nat_hole_resp` function creates a synthetic `NatHoleClient` message from the provider's `NatHoleResp` and calls `ctx.state.xtcp.nat_hole.handle_client(...)` on it. This is intended to store the provider's candidate addresses for the session, but it also triggers `session.notify_ch.send(())` which signals the waiting spawn task. If the real `NatHoleClient` from the provider already arrived and triggered the notify, the second `handle_client` call will see the oneshot already `take()`n (so `send()` returns Err). Additionally, `handle_nat_hole_resp` is called from the provider's control connection handler, while `handle_client` is normally called from the provider's control connection too — this creates an artificial two-path notification for the same event.
fix_suggestion: Instead of calling handle_client (which sends on notify_ch), create a dedicated method on Controller that only stores the provider addresses without signalling the notify channel. Or gate the notify_ch send behind a flag/check.

title: Rust build_nat_hole_response uses rsplit(':') which is incorrect for IPv6 candidate addresses
go_ref: pkg/nathole/controller.go:379-402 — getRangePorts uses net.SplitHostPort which handles IPv6 correctly
description: The Rust `build_nat_hole_response` function parses port from the last candidate address using `last_addr.rsplit(':').next()`. This is incorrect for IPv6 addresses like `[2001:db8::1]:12345` — `rsplit(':')` would split on the colons inside the IPv6 address and return the wrong port. The Go equivalent uses `net.SplitHostPort()` which correctly handles bracketed IPv6. The classifier's `split_host_port` in classify.rs handles IPv6 correctly, but the controller.rs code path does not.
fix_suggestion: Reuse the `split_host_port` function from classify.rs (or make it a public utility in the nathole module) instead of inline rsplit(':').
